results.title: Hugging Face Is Half Replicate's Price on A100 -- But the Gap Nearly Vanishes on H100
highlights:
4 November 2026 · Site Methodology & Pricing Notes · 5 min read

I was updating our Hugging Face and Replicate reference pages today and pulled both companies' current GPU pricing tables side by side for the first time. Same hardware -- same NVIDIA chips, same memory configs -- but two very different per-hour numbers. The surprise wasn't that they differ. It's that the size of the gap depends entirely on which GPU you pick.

## The numbers, checked today

Hugging Face Inference Endpoints bill dedicated, autoscaling GPUs by the hour. Replicate bills by the second, converted here to an hourly-equivalent rate so the two are directly comparable:

| GPU | Hugging Face $/hr | Replicate $/hr equiv. | Replicate premium |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T4 | $0.50 | $0.81 | +62% |
| L40S | $1.80 | $3.51 | +95% |
| A100 (80GB) | $2.50 | $5.04 | +102% |
| H100 | $4.50 | $5.49 | +22% |

On the three lower tiers, Replicate costs roughly double what the same chip costs on Hugging Face -- a 62-102% premium. Then on H100, the gap collapses to 22%. Whatever is driving the markup on T4 through A100 isn't driving it nearly as hard on H100.

## We can see the pattern, not the reason

Neither company publishes its underlying GPU acquisition cost, so this is a correlation we can verify from the public price tables, not a mechanism either side has confirmed. One plausible read: H100 capacity is the scarcest, most contested tier right now, and when demand is tight relative to supply, there's less room for either platform to price a markup on top of what the hardware itself costs them -- both get pushed toward something closer to the floor. On T4 and A100, older and more abundant chips, there's more slack for a convenience premium to survive. That's a plausible story, not a confirmed one.

## One tier Replicate doesn't sell at all

Hugging Face's table goes further than Replicate's: it lists H200 at $5.00/hr (1x) and B200 at $9.25/hr (1x) as selectable hardware. Replicate's public pricing page tops out at H100 -- no H200, no B200 row, as of this check. If a workload specifically needs either of those two chips, that's not a price comparison anymore; it's a one-sided option.

## Why the cheaper number isn't automatically the right pick

These are both real, per-hour-equivalent numbers, but they come from different billing models. Replicate charges per second only while a model is actually executing and scales to zero with no standing instance to manage -- idle time costs nothing, full stop. Hugging Face Inference Endpoints also scale to zero, but you're provisioning a dedicated endpoint rather than calling a stateless function; the hourly rate applies whenever that endpoint is up and serving, which depends on how your autoscaling is configured. For bursty, low-volume traffic with long idle gaps, Replicate's higher per-second rate can still land cheaper in practice than these hourly-equivalent numbers suggest -- the comparison above assumes continuous use on both sides, which is the fair way to compare the rate but not necessarily your real bill.

results.title: Replicate model hosting and serverless GPU pricing analysis - airtrain.ai
results.author: AI research
highlights:
Replicate offers a model marketplace with over 50,000 public models, but H100 instances cost $5.49 per hour, which is significantly higher than competitors like Modal or Runpod. The platform is ideal for rapid prototyping, though dedicated servers may…

...

I find Replicate the best option for quickly validating an AI product without managing infrastructure. Replicate acts as an "App Store for models" with over 50,000 public models available. You can use Cog packaging to turn your own model into an API. The platform allows developers to deploy models using a single command once the Cog package is ready. I recommend this for testing ideas quickly because you do not need to write deployment code. Replicate has attracted 30,000 paying customers, including companies like Buzzfeed and Unsplash, as well as startups like Character AI. The company recently closed a $40 million Series B round led by Andreessen Horowitz. Replicate aims to make machine learning accessible to every software developer through models that generate text, images, video, music, and speech. However, I find Replicate significantly more expensive than its competitors. An H100 costs $5.49 per hour, while Modal charges $3.95 per hour. For an H100, the price difference between Replicate and Runpod is 27%. An A100 80GB costs $5.04 per hour. For FLUX image generation, you pay between $0.025 and $0.04 per image. If you use a model that has not received requests recently, you face cold starts that add 10 to 60 seconds of latency.

results.title: Replicate's H100 Is Only 9% Pricier Than A100 Now — We Still Showed a 2x Gap
highlights:
# Replicate's H100 Is Only 9% Pricier Than A100 Now — We Still Showed a 2x Gap

24 October 2026 · Site Methodology & Corrections · 4 min read

Our Replicate pricing page has said A100 is $0.00115/second and H100 is $0.0025/second since July -- H100 costing more than double. I checked it against Replicate's own pricing page today. Both numbers are gone. The A100 40GB tier doesn't exist anymore, and H100 now runs at $0.001525/second -- barely above A100, not 117% above it.

## What actually changed

| Hardware | We had (July) | Real now | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A100 | $0.00115/s (40GB) | $0.0014/s (80GB) | 40GB tier retired, 80GB-only is 22% pricier |
| H100 | $0.0025/s | $0.001525/s | 39% cheaper |
| L40S | not listed | $0.000975/s | new tier, 30% cheaper than A100 |

Two separate things happened and they point in opposite directions, which is exactly why nobody notices both at once. A100 got more expensive because the cheap 40GB variant was pulled -- everyone building on A100 now defaults to the 80GB card whether their model needs that much memory or not. H100 got much cheaper, enough that it closed almost the entire gap to A100.

...

Our old numbers implied H100 costs 117% more than A100 -- a real deterrent if you were choosing hardware on a budget. The actual gap today is 9%. For anyone picking between the two for a model that runs on either, that's the difference between "H100 is a premium upgrade" and "H100 is basically the same price, take it." I'd been telling readers for three months to default to A100 unless they specifically needed H100's speed. That advice was built on a price gap that stopped being true at some point between July and now and I never re-checked it.

...

## Why I didn't catch this sooner

Replicate bills per second with no contract to review, no invoice that spells out "price changed" -- the rate just moves on the pricing page and your next bill reflects it. There's no renewal notice forcing a look, unlike a SaaS subscription. I'd verified this page once in July against the number that was live then and treated it as stable infrastructure pricing rather than something that needed the same periodic re-check as a volatile LLM token rate. GPU cloud pricing moves plenty -- it just doesn't announce itself.

## What I fixed

Updated the Replicate guide's table: A100 is now listed as 80GB only at $0.0014/second, H100 at $0.001525/second, and added the L40S row that was missing entirely. The per-1,000-run estimate column was also quietly assuming a 5-second job in the caption while the actual math used ~120 seconds -- fixed that caption to match reality too, since a 5-second caption next to a 120-second-implied number was its own small lie.

- Replicate pricing guide — corrected A100/H100/L40S rates, last verified 2026-10-24.
- Together AI — if you want GPU inference without picking a specific card yourself.
- Hugging Face Inference Endpoints — the closest rival for hosting a specific open model.

results.title: Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16 | GPUJournal
highlights:
Read on Lambda's own pricing page today, Nov 6, 2026: the Instances table now prints the prices that take effect on Nov 16, 2026 — HGX B200 up $1.00 an hour, H100 up $0.60 and A100 80GB up $0.40. It is the largest single announced rise we have caught this autumn, and renters have ten days' notice.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on lambda.ai/pricing

What was announced, in the pricing page's own words (read Nov 6, 2026): 'These prices take effect November 16, 2026, at 00:00 UTC. Until then, log in to your Lambda Cloud account to see current pricing.' The printed Nov 16 rates: HGX B200 $7.69 an hour (from the $6.69 last verified on Nov 5, +14.9%), HGX H100 $4.59 (from $3.99, +15.0%), HGX A100 80GB $3.19 (from $2.79, +14.3%), and HGX A100 40GB unchanged at $1.99. Lambda is also now at a new address — lambda.com — announced on its blog on Nov 5, 2026; the pricing page itself still answers at lambda.ai/pricing.

How we are treating it: an announced rise is not a live price. Our board keeps Lambda's last verified rates until Nov 16 and will move only when the new rates are re-verified in effect on or after that date — the rise is recorded in Price Watch today as announced, with both dates. One consequence of the announcement is already live, though: Lambda's currently-effective rates can no longer be read on its public page, only after logging in, so today's public check could verify the future rates but not re-read the current ones.

...

Its H100 at $4.59 would remain above the board's best H100 SXM offer (TensorDock, from $2.25 at an 8-GPU minimum) but move Lambda from the middle of the H100 pack toward its top.

results.title: Platts to launch US GPU Compute Prices, Nov. 23 | S&P Global
highlights:
Platts to launch US GPU Compute Prices, Nov. 23 | S&P Global 

 November 05, 2026

# Platts to launch US GPU Compute Prices, Nov. 23

Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, will launch US GPU Compute prices, effective Nov. 23, 2026.

Daily on-demand and interruptible prices will cover four NVIDIA chips: the NVIDIA H100, H200, B200 and B300 chips. Prices will be published in US dollars per GPU-hour and US dollars per million tokens of output, based on prices and availability at 1:30 pm CT.

COVERAGE

The assessments reflect the market value of available NVIDIA GPU compute capacity delivered through qualifying virtualized infrastructure services in the US by providers and marketplaces. The new assessments will capture an evolving segment of the compute market, where growing availability of dedicated GPU capacity and increasingly standardized service offerings have supported greater price transparency. The assessments will provide standardized price references for accessing GPU compute capacity in the US, adding further granularity to Platts coverage of the infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence workloads.

METHODOLOGY

Each GPU price will be a simple average of the prices of available GPUs for each chip and service type. Platts will review the prices for outliers and will automatically exclude any prices greater than 2 median absolute deviations from the median.

Platts may review the suitability of the current methodology and consider adopting a volume-weighted average approach once sufficient trade data has been collected. Platts encourages market participants to report trade data to ComputePricing@spglobal.com (PriceGroup@spglobal.com) for this purpose.

The symbols published will be as follows:

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Index, November 2026: H100 to B300
highlights:
Every month we check the public on-demand prices of specialist GPU clouds to set our own: CoreGPU prices every GPU at least 25% below the market median. This is the data behind that number, as listed on November 4, 2026.

## Method

- One on-demand price per provider and GPU, taken from public pricing pages or price APIs. Prices for 8-GPU nodes are divided by eight.
- Specialist GPU clouds only for the median. Hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle) are listed separately because their prices are 2.5 to 4.5 times higher.
- Monthly cost = hourly price × 730 hours. Prices exclude taxes.

## Median prices by GPU

| GPU | Prices found | Lowest $/h | Median $/h | Median / month |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA B300 | 8 | 6.60 | 8.98 | $6,552 |
| NVIDIA B200 | 11 | 5.43 | 8.19 | $5,979 |
| NVIDIA H200 | 12 | 2.90 | 4.94 | $3,606 |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM | 16 | 1.99 | 3.72 | $2,716 |
| NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 | 9 | 1.40 | 2.19 | $1,599 |
| NVIDIA L40S | 11 | 0.73 | 1.57 | $1,146 |
| AMD MI325X | 2 | 3.80 | 4.21 | $3,071 |
| AMD MI300X | 4 | 2.59 | 3.22 | $2,351 |

...

## Hyperscalers

On-demand prices per GPU-hour at the largest clouds remain far above specialist clouds: H100 from $6.88 (8-GPU instance divided by eight) to more than $12 depending on the provider, and B300 from $15 to $17.80. Commitments of one to three years cut those prices by 30 to 56%.

## What moved in 2026

- Prices are rising again for flagships. At least one large specialist cloud announced increases of 10 to 26% on H100, H200 and B300 from December 1.
- Clusters cost more than single instances. Multi-node offers are commonly 20 to 50% more per GPU than on-demand single servers.
- Listed is not available. Several providers list GPUs with no deployable region, or “contact sales” for every flagship.
- Fees moved to storage and idle time. Egress is mostly free; stopped-instance storage, public IPs and minimum billing periods are where extra cost appears.

results.title: The H100 got more expensive · Three Phase. Potentia Intelligence.
results.author: Jose Mir
highlights:
### One Big Thing · Phase 3 · Compute

What happened: Nebius raised on-demand GPU prices on October 1, its second hike in about three months. Independent trackers show the same direction across the market.

Why it matters: The bear case on AI infrastructure assumed GPUs lose value fast. Rental rates are the cleanest test of that assumption, and so far the test is failing.

By the numbers:

- Nebius list price for an H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour; B300 from $7.85 to $9.50.
- The Ornn H100 index settled at $3.17 on October 23, up about 4% in a month.

results.title: Nebius and CoreWeave Lift Nvidia GPU Prices by Up to 21% - Economic Frame
highlights:
Nvidia rental prices are rising even for last-generation H100s. Nebius has posted an October 1, 2026 on-demand card that lifts selected Nvidia GPU-hour rates by 16.9% to 21.0%. CoreWeave said on September 17 that it is still signing compute at higher prices, including short contracts at about $40 million per megawatt of annualized revenue. A landlord can charge more for a chip it does not make only while that chip stays scarce. That is the signal behind Nvidia, and it is the opposite of a capacity glut.

Nebius’s price page, checked on October 2, still prints two columns. On-demand H100 is $3.85 per GPU-hour. The column marked effective October 1 is $4.50. The same split runs through the H200, the B200, and the B300. Reuters reported on September 17 that this was the second pay-as-you-go increase in about three months, with selected Nvidia GPU rates up 17% to 21%. The card on nebius.com/prices matches that range. It does not show every customer already paying the new rate.

## The card Nebius posted

Four Nvidia rows have a public before and after. GB200 NVL72 and GB300 NVL72 racks are still “contact us” in both columns. RTX PRO 6000 stays at $1.80. L40S “from” rates do not move. The hike lands on the accelerators customers are queued for.

| Nvidia GPU | Prior on-demand column | Announced October 1 card | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HGX H100 | $3.85 | $4.50 | +$0.65, or 16.9% |
| HGX H200 | $4.50 | $5.40 | +$0.90, or 20.0% |
| HGX B200 | $7.15 | $8.50 | +$1.35, or 18.9% |
| HGX B300 | $7.85 | $9.50 | +$1.65, or 21.0% |

Reuters’ “17% to 21%” is this range, with 16.9% rounded up. “Up to 21%” is the B300. The smaller H100 move is the one that changes the reading. Hopper is not the generation Nvidia is leading with. A prior-generation accelerator getting more expensive to rent is not what surplus hardware looks like.

...

Announced Nebius on-demand rates for October 1, 2026, set against the prior on-demand column still printed on the same page. These are posted card rates, not a receipt. The live page and a third-party tracker still disagree, so this chart does not show what every customer is paying. Source: nebius.com/prices, checked October 2, 2026.

...

## The announced column is not yet the only column

October 2 is after the effective date, and the page still shows both numbers. The left-hand label is still “On-demand, GPU-hour.” The right-hand label is “GPU-hour (Effective October 1, 2026).” A customer cannot tell, from the page alone, which figure the console will bill.

GPU Finder’s Nebius page, with availability checked at 06:23 UTC on October 2, still listed one-GPU on-demand rates of $3.85 for the H100, $7.15 for the B200, and $7.85 for the B300. Those are the old column. The same check already showed the H200 at $5.40, the new column, with a spot print of $2.45 beside it. The H100 spot print on that row was $2.15. The tracker has not frozen. It has moved one of the four headline GPUs and left the other three on the pre-October number. Treating the whole book as repriced at midnight on October 1 would be tidier, and it would be wrong.

Commitment discounts can run up to 35% below on-demand for large clusters reserved for multiple months. Full discount on the new H100 card is $2.93 an hour, under the old $3.85 list. On the new B300 card it is $6.18, under $7.85. “Up to” is not “everyone gets.” The headline increase is the unreserved rate.

results.title: The Price of a GPU-Hour Is Now Set by Memory, Not Compute | AIChieve
results.author: Jorge Fernandez Ilufi
highlights:
Cloud provider Nebius raised its hourly rate for an Nvidia H100 chip from $3.85 to $4.50 on October 1, 2026, while pushing the newer B200 to $8.50. 

Cloud provider Nebius raised its hourly rate for an Nvidia H100 chip from $3.85 to $4.50 on October 1, 2026, while pushing the newer B200 to $8.50 [3]. The chips did not get faster, but their memory now costs much more. Two days prior, TrendForce raised its 2027 forecast for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to a 121% jump over this year’s prices [1].

...

- 121% — HBM price jump: TrendForce expects the blended price of high-bandwidth memory to rise 121% next year due to tight supply and a shift to the newest HBM4 grade [1].
- 17% to 21% — Nebius rate hike: The cloud provider raised H100 rates to $4.50, H200 to $5.40, B200 to $8.50, and B300 to $9.50 per GPU-hour on October 1, 2026 [3].
- $8.55 vs $14.24 — B200 spread: An independent tracker puts the median on-demand B200 at $8.55 an hour at dedicated GPU clouds and $14.24 at large hyperscalers [5].
- 10% to 15% — DRAM contracts: TrendForce expects standard DRAM contract prices to climb another 10% to 15% in the fourth quarter [2].

...

What strikes me is that the price of the newest chip relies entirely on how much memory it holds, not how much math it does. A September index tracking rental rates put the B200 at $8.01 an hour [4]. It reported the chip now costs 21% more per unit of compute than the older H100 [4].
